newsitem.title: USA: Dissent vote seen as early signal of FOMC moves.
newsitem.headline: Dissent vote seen as early signal of FOMC moves.

text.p: Since it launched a preemptive anti-inflation tightening cycle in February 1994, the Federal Reserve has steadily changed interest rates in the direction of a dissenting vote cast at a prior Federal Open Market Committee meeting, Fed records show.
The latest dissent on public record is the vote for an immediate tightening of credit cast by Minneapolis Fed Bank President Gary Stern at the July 2-3 FOMC gathering.
In his dissent, Stern voiced concern the economy is expanding at a pace that may become inflationary.

A number of Fed officials have since echoed Stern's need for anti-inflation vigilance as the Fed kept the 5.25-percent federal funds rate unchanged at its August policy-setting meeting despite an existing bias to tighten credit.
The Minneapolis Fed district enjoys a pace of economic activity above the national average and an unemployment rate so low that its region's Beige Book coined the phrase "discouraged employers."
Fed bank presidents, however, like the central bank's governors, are generally seen forming their policy views based on national considerations.

"FOMC members rarely dissent unless they feel there is some sentiment in the Committee in support of their views. They feel that sentiment deserves to be recognized," said Lou Crandall, chief economist at Wrightson and Associates.
Fed Governors Wayne Angell and Lawrence Lindsey dissented in favor of an immediate tightening at the December 21, 1993, FOMC meeting which left rates unchanged without a policy bias.

The FOMC raised the federal funds rate, then at 3.0 percent, by 25 basis points at its ensuing February 3-4, 1994, meeting, ushering in a tightening cycle whose pace was among the most aggressive in Fed history, given the inflation rate.

Richmond Fed President Alfred Broaddus and Cleveland Fed President Jerry Jordan dissented in favor of a more aggressive move at the March 22, 1994, FOMC when the Fed raised the funds rate again by 25 basis points with no bias.
The Fed hiked the overnight bank lending rate by another 25 points on April 18, 1994 -- the only inter-meeting move since the prior easing cycle that started in mid-1989.

Broaddus again dissented in favor of an immediate tightening at the July 5-6, 1994, FOMC meeting when the Fed did not move but introduced a tightening bias. The FOMC raised rates by 50 basis points at the August 16, 1994, confab.
Broaddus dissented once more for an immediate tightening at the September 27, 1994, gathering when the Fed left rates unchanged and did not introduce a tightening bias.
The Fed raised the funds rate by 75 basis points at the ensuing meeting, with no bias.

"What this seems to suggest is that (FOMC members) are very careful about assessing the (economic) environment before making a policy change. It's a very intriguing pattern," said managing director Ward McCarthy at Stone and McCarthy Research Associates of Princeton, N.J. "This would suggest they will make a decision (to move) at next week's meeting."
The FOMC is set to meet on Tuesday, September 24.
In the final dissent of the 1994 cycle, Governor John LaWare voted for an immediate tightening at the December 20 FOMC meeting when the Fed left rates unchanged with no policy bias.
The Fed raised rates by 50 basis points at the following February 1, 1995, meeting and did not adopt a bias.

"If you look at the composition of the FOMC at any point in time, there are typically (inflation) doves and there are hawks," said McCarthy. He added that it probably takes a little more time and signs of economic strength or weakness to sway the doves or the hawks in either direction.
There was no dissent at the May 23, 1995, FOMC meeting, when the Fed left rates unchanged with no bias despite signs the expansion might be slowing at a faster-than-desired pace.
The Fed, citing the improving performance of inflation, shaved 25 points off the then 6.0-percent funds rate at the following July 5-6 FOMC meeting.

However, a Fed source told Reuters that then-Fed Vice Chairman Alan Blinder -- an expert on inventories who had been concerned about their build-up -- had made it known he would dissent if the Fed did not ease in July.

At the November 15, 1995, FOMC meeting, when the Fed did not ease nor introduce a bias, Lindsey dissented for an immediate rate cut -- which was adopted at the December 19, 1995, meeting, again on the grounds of improving inflation.

No dissent was recorded at the December meeting and no bias was introduced. The Fed, however, eased the funds rate another notch and lowered the discount rate on January 31, 1996 -- the latest of its moves -- as six Fed banks requested a discount rate cut.
